reasoning: The two best performers so far are the psychology reel (reach 30, 2 likes, lowest skip rate at 51.7) and the 'body in space' reel (reach 24). Both are evergreen niche reels with mystery music, so I'm staying in psychology with a new topic: false and rewritten memories. It is personal, a little unsettling and easy to share. I chose a reel because reels are the only format that has reached more than 10 people so far, and I kept it to 5 slides as the strategy says. This is also version B of the reel hook test: the hook states the shocking claim directly instead of asking a question, so it can be compared with the psychology reel. I kept the mystery music and palette 3 (the same as the best psychology reel) so the hook is the main thing that changes. I did not make it a trial reel: with 0 followers all reach already comes from non-followers, so a trial adds nothing yet. Every fact comes from well-documented studies: Loftus & Palmer 1974, Loftus & Pickrell 1995, Talarico & Rubin 2003 and research on memory reconsolidation.
topic: False memories: reconsolidation, leading words, planted memories, flashbulb confidence
hook: Your memories change every time you recall them

slides.title: Recall rewrites it
slides.body: Each time you remember something, your brain rebuilds the memory and can store it back slightly changed.
slides.image_prompt: A glass sculpture of a human brain cracked into pieces, glowing threads of light stitching the fragments back together on a dark background

slides.title: One word changes it
slides.body: People asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other guessed higher speeds than those asked how fast they 'hit'.
slides.image_prompt: Two vintage toy cars touching bumpers on a dark table under a dramatic spotlight, shards of light scattered around them

slides.title: Glass that never was
slides.body: A week later, 32% of the 'smashed' group remembered broken glass. The crash film showed none.
slides.image_prompt: Shards of broken glass floating in dark empty space, half transparent like a fading dream, soft blue light

slides.title: Planted memories
slides.body: In a 1995 study, about 1 in 4 adults came to remember being lost in a mall as kids. It never happened.
slides.image_prompt: An empty, dimly lit shopping mall corridor seen through fog, a small lost red balloon floating near the ceiling

slides.title: Confidence lies too
slides.body: After 9/11, people's memories of that day drifted like ordinary memories, yet they stayed just as sure they were right.
slides.image_prompt: An old photograph slowly dissolving into dust at one corner, resting on a dark wooden desk under a single warm lamp

cta: Follow so you never miss the next one
caption:
Your memories are not recordings. Every time you recall one, your brain rebuilds it and can save it back with small changes. In one classic study, a single word, 'smashed' instead of 'hit', made people remember broken glass that was never there.

This is not just a lab curiosity. According to the Innocence Project, eyewitness misidentification played a role in about 69% of US wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA evidence. (Sources: Loftus & Palmer 1974, Loftus & Pickrell 1995, Talarico & Rubin 2003)
